A squat riveted boiler stands at the end of the house with its firedoor cracked open and glowing, a fat brass steam main rising from its crown and turning away down the beds; a brass safety valve on the crown lifts and sighs off a little steam, and the coal is heaped loose beside it in a plain iron bin.

Brass steam pipes thread between the beds at shin height, lagged in tarred cloth where they pass the walkway, and at one elbow joint a bright white plume is venting steadily up into the leaves overhead; a small brass wheel-valve sits where the line splits three ways.

The ridge vents stand cranked half open the whole length of the roof, each sash lifted by a jointed iron arm off one long shaft, and the drive chain comes down the near pier to a big spoked hand-wheel at waist height with its handle worn bright.

A rotating irrigation arm creeps slowly over the central bed on a brass pivot column, a thin drizzle falling from the pierced pipe along its whole length and darkening the soil in a curved band where it has already passed.

High under the ridge a hand-cranked fan as broad as a wagon wheel turns slowly on a brass hub, its varnished canvas blades stirring the steam into slow spirals, the crank shaft running down to a handle on the wall.

Copper condensation channels run along the foot of every glazed flank, brimming and busy with clear water, and they empty through a spout into a green-stained copper cistern sunk into the brick floor.
Under the iron floor grating a big hot-water main runs the length of the house, and steam escapes up between the slats in soft white ribbons that thin out around the ankles of the nearest plants.
A bank of brass bell-jars on a plumbed rail, each one sweating on the inside and dripping into its own little copper saucer, the drips falling out of time with each other.
A chain hoist hangs from the ironwork with a crated specimen swinging a hand's breadth off the floor, the chain's slack looped over a cleat and the lifting hook still bearing the weight.
A brass pressure governor spins on top of the steam main, two heavy balls flying out level, and a linkage from it holds the throttle valve exactly where it wants to be.
A propagating bench with copper pipes buried in warm sand beneath it, the sand steaming faintly along the whole bench and the pipes turning up at the end into a brass return elbow.
A pedal-driven bellows stands beside the boiler with its leather lung half collapsed, the treadle plate polished by use and an air trunk running from it into the firebox.
A clockwork blind winds itself slowly across the roof panes on a brass drum and cords, half the glass shaded and half still clear, the drum turning with a soft steady tick of pawls.
A brass misting rail runs above the fern tiers on slim brackets, throwing a fine drift of water that hangs in the air, so fine it drifts instead of falling.
A water ram thumps away in the corner behind the potting bench, a heavy soft knock every few seconds, its brass dome bright where hands have rubbed it and its outlet pipe dribbling.
An overhead sprinkler ring of perforated brass hangs above the lily pool, rain falling from it in a perfect circle onto the pads and pocking the water inside the ring only.
A great square hot-air trunk climbs the inner wall with louvred flaps down its face, and the flaps are snapping open one after another as the heat rises behind them.
A copper worm coil sits submerged in an open tank of water, steam rolling off the surface in a low white blanket and the coil's inlet hissing softly where it enters.
Rack-and-pinion vent openers march along the ridge, brass teeth engaged, every sash raised to exactly the same angle, one of them stiff and standing a finger's width lower than the rest.
A brass syphon feeds the pool from a header tank on iron legs, a bright rope of water falling clear from its spout with a steady trembling in it.
A valve wheel taller than a person stands where two steam mains join, its rim wrapped in worn rope for grip, a small dribble of condensate running from the gland below it.

A steam-driven revolving stand turns one potted specimen slowly in the brightest part of the floor, its brass turntable whispering round and a fine drive belt running down to a little engine underneath.
A soot-blackened iron flue climbs the inner wall from the boiler to the roof, warm enough that the moss growing at its foot has dried to a pale ring, and a cloth is draped over its lowest bracket.

A brass float-and-lever regulator stands on the pier, its copper float riding high on the water in an open box and the long counterweighted lever holding the inlet shut, every part of it beaded with condensate.
A night-heater brazier on iron wheels has been pushed in among the tender beds, its stovepipe elbowed up into the roof space, the coals inside still red and ticking.

A brass reducing valve crouches on the main steam line where it enters the house proper, its bonnet cap green with age and a steady bead of condensate gathering at the lower flange and dropping into the brick channel below.

Iron radiator coils run beneath the staging on both sides of the house, their painted surfaces blistered and rust-streaked where the paint has lifted, and they tick and ping as the steam moves through them in surges.

Two parallel brass slide-valves sit side by side on a shared manifold bolted to the pier, each with its own small lever locked upright, and a thin mineral crust has formed around every thread and joint.

A leather drive belt runs from a small flywheel on the boiler shaft up to a pulley overhead, slapping against its own slack on every revolution and leaving a faint smell of hot leather in the warm air.
Long canvas shading blinds hang in doubled rolls along the south flank, lowered to half height and tied off on brass cleats, their lower hems swaying in the draught from the open vents.

A soil-warming tray of riveted copper sits on the lower bench, its lid perforated with close holes, a rubber hose coupling it to the brass steam line below with a loop of slack hose pooling on the floor.
A mercury thermometer in a perforated brass case stands on a spike driven into the central bed, its tube climbing to the second red mark from the top, the brass cage greening at its rim.
The main cistern overflow pipe arcs out through the base of the back wall, and a steady thin stream falls from its lip into the brick gutter outside, the brick face below it dark and permanently wet.

An iron hand-pump on a flanged base stands beside the cistern, its lever worn to bare metal along the grip, a drip of water hanging at the spout lip and the pump rod shining where the packing gland grips it.
Wrought-iron staging brackets carry the upper bench along the whole east wall, and under each bracket a small brass clip holds the heating pipe tight against the fascia so it cannot swing free.

A coiled brass expansion loop sits midway along the long steam main, its bend creaking softly as the pipe shifts with the heat, and a patch of fresh white lime on the wall behind it marks where it once touched.
A small steam trap of brass and iron sits at the lowest point of the run, its outlet pipe dripping condensate in slow fat drops into a groove worn in the brick floor beneath it.
A glass-and-brass hygrometer hangs from the ridge ironwork on a short brass rod, its two hair-strands visible behind the dial face, and the needle rests a little past the middle of the scale.
The boiler feed pipe runs back from the pump along the outer wall on cast-iron brackets, lagged in plaster-and-hessian wrap that has cracked open at one joint and shows the bright copper pipe inside.
A small iron trolley carries a copper dosing tank on a slatted timber deck, its brass tap at the base still dripping faintly and the whole trolley sitting slightly tilted on the uneven floor.
Perforated clay field pipes are laid end to end under the gravel of the central bed, and along their run the gravel is darkened with slow upwelling moisture that spreads outward from the centre.

Four large cast-iron weights hang from the ridge ventilator counterbalance rod on hooks of different sizes, the rod itself bowing gently under their combined load and the highest weight swinging a little with any draught.
A brass lubricator cup sits on the top of the fan shaft bearing, its glass reservoir still half full of pale oil, a thin dark trail of overflow dried down the outside of the bearing housing.

Copper tie-rods run diagonally between the main frame piers, threaded at each end into a cast boss, and the rods have gone a deep brown-green except where a spanner has recently gripped the flats of the turnbuckles.

An iron drip tray bolted under the pipe junction catches the condensate there, and it is full to the brim, brimming so steadily that a thin sheet runs over one corner and follows the brick face down to the floor.

A small bellcrank lever on the back wall connects by a long brass rod to the damper inside the flue, and the lever is set in a slotted quadrant with a pin dropped through one of the holes to hold the damper partly open.

A pair of copper spray lances hang on brass hooks beside the potting bench, their pump barrels of polished brass and their nozzle caps different sizes, both nozzles still wet and dripping onto the shelf below.

The main steam header runs across the far gable end at head height on heavy iron brackets, lagged in white-painted plaster that has yellowed near every joint, and a single pressure gauge hangs from it on a short brass spur.

A gravity hot-water circulator of cast iron sits beside the boiler, its body ribbed on all sides, and the upper flow pipe climbs in a wide slow curve across the wall before dividing into the two bed runs.

A chain of small brass inspection caps runs along the top of the condensate return main, each cap square-headed and each one slightly different in its degree of tarnish, the most recent one still clean enough to show its casting marks.

A brass injector valve clicks on the steam main near the boiler end, a thin jet of water audible inside the pipe body, and the union nut around it is dark with old hemp jointing that has swollen tight against the thread.
Cast iron radiator fins run the length of the far wall in a low row, each fin painted black and too hot to hold, a soft metallic ticking moving along them as the steam pressure shifts.
Coiled copper tubing wraps a clay pot on the warm bench, warm enough that the terracotta above the coil has dried to a lighter band while the clay below stays dark with moisture.
A lead cistern bolted to the ironwork overhead sweats on every surface, the condensate gathering and dripping in a slow curtain onto the broad leaves of the bed directly below.

An iron gear wheel turns on a wall-mounted bracket, its teeth meshing with a smaller pinion that drives the long horizontal shaft running to the roof vent openers, the grease on the teeth black and glossy.

The staging iron pipe runs along the back of the bench, and from it a row of individual copper branch pipes curves down to each pot in a regular series, each one pinned shut by a small brass thumbscrew.
Steam curls from the open top of the condensate pot sunk into the floor at the boiler end, the pot's iron rim level with the grating and dark with scale around its edge.
A pair of brass pressure gauges face each other on the steam main, one reading higher than the other, their white faces fogged on the inside and their needles trembling faintly.
A slide-valve chest sits along the top of the small engine block below the turntable, a thin seam of steam showing at one end of its face plate and the valve rod visible through the inspection notch.
Iron shutters are folded back against the outer piers in the morning position, their hinges streaked orange and their inner faces bright where they reflect heat back from the beds in summer.
A rope and pulley drops from the apex ironwork to the centre of the roof ventilator spindle, the rope's end knotted to an iron ring bolted into the timber lintel at eye height.
Mineral scale has built up around the base of every irrigation fitting in a white crust, thickest at the lowest bracket where a slow drip has run for a long season.

An iron standpipe rises in the corner with a brass bib tap halfway up its length, a rubber hose coiled on the peg beside it and the tap left a quarter open so a thin thread of water falls into the drain.

The hotbed frame against the south wall is heated by a brick flue running beneath the soil, the soil surface several degrees warmer than the path, a faint shimmer of heat visible when the angle of the light is right.
A long brass draw-off cock stands at the low end of the boiler, its handle set sideways for closed, a shallow iron tray placed underneath it that has caught a little rusty water.
Soot has collected in the angle between the flue collar and the roof iron in a soft black shelf, and where heat has dried it, it has cracked into a fine map of lines.
An iron winding frame on the near wall carries several loops of chain on its drum, each chain running up to a different roof section, the drum ratcheted still with a clicking pawl bar.
Expansion loops of copper pipe are bent flat against the top of the glazing bars in a wide U at each end of the main runs, the metal bright on the outer bend where it flexes.
The brick pier beside the boiler carries a full set of tapped bosses for the branch feeds, some filled with blank plugs and some with live valves, all of them dripping at the flange joint.
A brick sump under the tile floor takes the overflow from the condensation channels and a slow trickle runs across the floor toward it, following a groove worn into the tile over many seasons.
A small centrifugal pump on a baseplate bolted near the cistern throbs with a low steady vibration, its discharge pipe trembling, and a thin bead of water runs from the gland along the shaft.
An iron inspection hatch in the floor stands propped open on its rod, the hot-water main visible inside the void below, lagged in a grey material and glowing faintly from reflected heat.
A series of copper heat fins are soldered along the underside of the propagation bench pipes, the fins close together and dark with condensate, transferring warmth upward into the sand.
The timber staging above the main bed has been fitted with iron angle brackets at each joint, and white mineral stains have run from each bracket down the face of the nearest board.
A long iron lever hinged at the wall controls the main damper inside the boiler flue, its far end resting on a notched iron quadrant bolted to the brickwork, the lever settled in the third notch.

A brass steam trap sits below the main run where a low point has collected condensate, its body warm to the touch and a slow drip falling from the discharge nipple onto the brick below in a dark spreading stain.

Iron tie-rods cross the width of the house near the eaves, each one drawn tight by a turnbuckle of bright steel, and along one rod a row of hanging baskets has been suspended on brass S-hooks at even spacing.
A copper soil-warming plate the size of a door lies flat under the seed trays, its surface crusted with lime at the edges and the steam inlet fitting at the near corner ticking softly as it heats.

The condensate return pipe runs back along the floor to the boiler at a slight downward pitch, held in saddle clips on low iron stands, and a line of small wet patches on the brick marks each clip where a little water has pooled.
A glass storm lantern hangs from a low bracket between two beds, its flame burning steady and warm inside the glasshouse air, the brass collar at its rim turned to the open position.
Beside the lily pool a brass hand pump stands on its own iron pedestal, the spout curved down to the water, the piston rod worn smooth and the leather cup at the base dripping after recent use.
A cast-iron wheel barrow loaded with crocks and grit stands at the junction of two paths, its tray floor rusted to a deep orange and a trace of wet soil on each wheel from the bed it was last worked.
A rack of terracotta forcing pots hangs on a wrought-iron frame above the hot-air trunk, each pot open at the top and the inside walls beaded with moisture from the warm air rising past them.
Two steam mains run side by side under the eaves, the smaller one lagged in white-painted canvas and the larger left bare, its copper surface blotched green and brown along the whole run.
A brass reducing union joins the fat steam main to a narrow spur, the body of the fitting bulging slightly where it was cast and a ring of older pipe compound dried brown at both joints.

An iron coal scuttle sits open beside the flue with a long-handled shovel resting across its rim, a dusting of fine black coal slack spread on the brickwork around it and a few small lumps on the floor.
A copper expansion loop bows out from the pipe run in a wide U, its bright surface dulled at the elbows where the metal flexes and a small bracket on the near pier giving it just enough play.
A hinged inspection cover on the floor grating stands propped open with an iron rod, the dark space below lit faintly orange by the heat pipes running through it and a smell of hot cast iron rising.

A small steam-pressure gauge is fitted to the branch pipe above the fern bench, its brass case fogged on the inside of the glass and the needle resting a little above the lowest mark on the dial face.
An iron roller the width of the central path leans against the pier, its surface chalked pale from the path material and the handle bar dark with rust except where hands have polished the grip.
Copper draw-off taps run at regular intervals along the base of the header tank, each one dripping a thin thread of water into a narrow channel that leads to the beds below.
A leather drive belt runs from a small flywheel on the boiler down through an iron floor grating to a shaft below, the belt greasy and flapping slightly at its join where it passes the upper pulley.

The pit bed in the centre of the house is lined with brick to a depth not quite visible from the path, a slow steam rising from the tanner's bark packed into it and the nearest pots sitting on iron staging above the pit mouth.

A cast-iron damper plate stands in a brass frame where the flue enters the outer wall, its handle pointing across the pipe run and a streamer of soot dust on the brickwork below the joint showing where the draw has been strong.
A brass blow-down cock is fitted to the boiler's lowest point, its handle wired open a crack so a thin stream of grey water runs out into a soakaway channel in the floor and carries the silt with it.

An open copper funnel on a bracket above the sand bench collects the drip from the overhead pipes and a thin bead of water runs from its spout down a copper rod into the sand below, drawn in at once without pooling.

A hand-wheel on the pier controls the sluice across the condensate channel, the wheel's iron spokes filmed with lime and the wooden block of the sluice swelled tight in its slot and dark with constant wet.

A set of nested bell-glasses of diminishing size sits stacked on the potting shelf, the largest misted entirely and the smallest clear, all of them giving off a faint warmth from the bench heating beneath them.

The wrought-iron staging along the south flank carries a double tier of specimen pots, the lower shelf close to the warm floor and the upper out in the full light, a drip rail of bent copper at the edge of each shelf catching the overflow.

A heavy brass stop-valve has been wedged fully open with a loop of wire through its spokes, the gland leaking enough that a white salt crust has formed on the pipe below it and a single drop hangs ready at the lowest point of the crust.
